newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. flies refugees from Zaire, sends new train.
newsitem.headline: U.N. flies refugees from Zaire, sends new train.

text.p: Nearly 1,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees flew home from Zaire on Tuesday and a train left to pick up more refugees two days after 91 died in a stampede.
Peter Kessler, spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR, said the train from Kisangani had more than 25 aid workers on board to help organise refugee loading.
He said the train's departure to Biaro camp, 41 km (25 miles) south, was delayed for an escort from the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Cong-Zaire (AFDL).
"Finally the alliance said no escort was needed and they (rebels) were prepared to take full responsibility," he said. "We expect it back at about five p.m. with as many as it can safely carry."
He said 900 refugees had left Kisangani so far on Tuesday aboard three Ilyushin planes for the Rwandan capital of Kigali.
"We are at about 8,400 since the airlift began on April 27 and hope to break 10,000 by the end of the day," said Kessler, adding UNHCR had sent five trucks to Biaro for sick and wounded.
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda the same year.
UNHCR on Monday blamed a breakdown in coordination with local rebel authorities for the death of the 91 Rwandan Hutu refugees who were crushed or suffocated on the train on Sunday.

"These arrangements did not move with full coordination," said Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees. "The military on the ground and our office were not really coordinated because of the difficulty of coordination as such."
Ogata said rebel authorities ordered the train on Sunday to leave Biaro without UNHCR clearance because too many people were on board.
A UNHCR report said refugees swarmed on board the six open cars of the train at two stops, where as many as 5,000 to 6,000 people were waiting to board.
Survivors said thousands of refugees swarmed onto the train as it pulled out of a station near Biaro camp. Children, the weak and ill adults were forced to the bottom of the metal cars.
The train on Tuesday was the first since Sunday's tragedy.
Rwanda's government on Tuesday demanded an international inquiry into the train disaster and blamed it on "gross inefficiency and mismanagement" by UNHCR.

Ephraim Kabaija, the head of Rwanda's joint commission for repatriation, said in a statement the refugees panicked because they had heard UNHCR intended to suspend the trains because its transit camp near Kisangani airport was full.

"The government is strongly concerned by this act of negligence and further urges the United Nations to stop the acts that prolong the suffering of the Rwandese," said Kabaija, adding Rwanda objected to anything slowing the refugee return.
U.N. officials said on Monday they had to plead with rebel authorities not to immediately resume evacuation of the Hutu refugees by rail.

Up to 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees south of Kisangani fled into the jungle two weeks ago after attacks by what they said were local Zaireans and rebels. Thousands have emerged in the last week, desperate to join the airlift to their homeland.
After weeks of delaying a U.N. airlift via Kisangani, citing a cholera outbreak, rebels said on April 27 U.N. agencies had 60 days from May 1 to repatriate all Rwandan refugees in Zaire.
